input.content:
Batch 14 Landed

Climb batch 14's final report: whether it landed, what it changed in Fortress, what it cost, how the work went, what's for your review, and what comes next.

STAMP

The answer

Yes. All five fixes landed on main at 05:34 UTC today (07:34 yours). A fix is one change, built by a worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a skeptic, a second agent that corrects what it finds.

The gate, the full test run before a landing, was green: 1.9K fast tests, 604 system tests and 130 specification examples, with no failure. microGPT's two quick checks under walk, the interpreter, passed 7 of 7 each.

The distance went from 85 to 54, exactly as the batch's plan said. The distance is the number of errors that the checker, the compiled path's type checker, reports on the one library: the interpreter's library, which the compiled path takes over at the switch-over. The count, the older measure that stops at a component's first error, stayed at 1.

It cost 4.82M tokens written, which are input plus cache writes, with cached reads left out. The plan said about 5.9M, and batch 13 cost 7.22M. It ran 4 h 43 min, with 14 agents.

Sources

1. The landing commit 7c2c7cd4b, 05:34 UTC, and its message. The five fixes' own commits: the gather's RECORD.md, “The landed commits”.

2. gate/summary.txt: testFast 1,945 tests in 48 suites, testSystem 604, testSpecData 130, 42 of 42 atomic runs, and the two “microgpt-walk VERDICT: 7 PASS, 0 FAIL of 7” lines.

3. gate/distance.txt (“#total 54”) and gate/checker-count.txt (“#total 1”); summary.txt, “DISTANCE DOWN 85 -> 54” and “COUNT SAME 1”. The plan's “about 54, the count 1”: CLIMB-BATCH-14.md, section 1, “Where the distance stands”. “Met to the site”: batch-14-review.md, section 1.

4. The review, section 2: 4.82M by the coordinator's spend.py, 14 agents, a span of 4 h 43. The plan's figure: CLIMB-BATCH-14.md, section 1, “Cost”.

What changed in Fortress

The checker reads self in a self-typed trait. A self-typed trait is a generic trait whose parameter stands for the type that implements it, like trait StandardTotalOrder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]. In its method bodies the checker now types self as both the trait and T, so the library's opr MAX(self, other: T): T = if other < self then self else other end is accepted, and 29 errors like it went with the library's text unchanged. In return, a type that extends such a trait must be that type: object generator extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\] is refused, since a generator isn't a trip.

The checker retries a call written as another call's argument. When no declaration of a call fits, an argument that's itself a generic call is checked again, with each declaration's parameter type as the type it should produce. So with mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\] and takesBox64(b: BoxT[\ZZ64\]), takesBox64(mk()) now compiles and makes a BoxT[\ZZ64\], where before it was refused. A declaration that fits the arguments as first typed is still never passed over, and no library error moved.

Three library repairs, and one line held. Array2's offset now checks its bounds the way Array1's does, and each fixed-size integer type declares its own numerator: 2 errors went. IntMap's SYMDIFF, the entries in exactly one of two maps, now works with a one-entry map: {0 |-> 0, 1 |-> 1, 2 |-> 2} SYMDIFF {5 |-> 5} holds all four entries, where it held only {2 |-> 2, 5 |-> 5}. The library's big-operator function keeps its one untyped parameter, because walk refuses the typed line.

The 2019 paper's examples are tests, and walk computes powers in sizes. The worked examples of the type group's POPL 2019 paper are now 27 test programs on both paths, the failing ones written as expected failures: tests named XXX that pass while the gap is there. Walk now computes a power in a size, so Box[\2^3\] has size 8, and it refuses a negative exponent, where before it stopped on any power. The specification's No Duplicates Rule now says, as the papers do, that two declarations may not each apply to every call the other applies to; the checker already refused such a pair, like dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\]) beside dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\]).

Walk's rule for an inherited abstract method is coverage. Walk refuses an object at load if it leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, and now the object's bodies at narrower types must together cover the method's parameter types, reading comprises lists, which name every case of a trait. So with trait D comprises { P, Q } and an abstract f(self, other: D), bodies at other: P and other: Q are enough. Before, any one narrower body was, and a call outside it stopped the program at run time; three library places in Random and QuickCheck that leaned on that got their bodies first.

Sources

1. Commit 1c32ccffd. The body: Library/FortressLibrary.fss, lines 281 to 293. The 29 sites by trait: the review, section 1. The refused object: ProjectFortress/demos/trips.fss, lines 97 and 98. The text: Specification/basic/traits.tex.

2. Commit 0856f3e6a. The example: compiler_tests/InferCallArgumentContext.fss. No site moved: the review, Part 1, rung A.

3. Commit 604d0e23c; rung-library-followups/REPORT.md, sections 1 and 2. The old and new values: tests/IntMapSymdiffSingleton.fss, line 12, and the gather's record, “Points to report”, rung L.

4. Commit 3ba2d005f; 15 walk and 12 compiled programs: the gather's record, “Handover lines”. tests/NatArithPowerWalk.fss; compiler_tests/NoDuplicatesRule.fss; the rule's old and new text: rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md, section 4.

5. Commit f9fe5c874. tests/AbstractMethodCoveredWalk.fss and tests/AbstractMethodPartlyDefinedWalk.fss; rung-walk-coverage/REPORT.md.

The cost

The batch wrote 4.82M tokens. That's 1.08M, or 18%, under the plan's 5.9M, and 2.4M under batch 13.

By role, for batches 11, 12 and 13, then this one:

  • Workers, who build the fixes: 1.99M, 2.05M, 2.64M, then 1.99M.
  • Skeptics: 1.60M, 1.67M, 2.59M, then 1.71M.
  • Judges, who rule when a skeptic's edit is contested: 140K, 300K, 455K, then none.
  • The gather, which lands the approved fixes on main and writes the batch's record: 486K, 527K, 592K, then 460K.
  • The merged-diff review, which reads the fixes together: 412K, 470K, 482K, then 399K.
  • The gate: 116K, 125K, 142K, then 131K.
  • The cold read, a fresh agent's read of the batch's new record entries: 154K, 155K, 168K, then dropped.
  • The commit, which records the gate's tables and pushes: 135K, 140K, 149K, then 128K.
  • In all: 5.03M, 5.43M, 7.22M, then 4.82M.

Per fix, with every role counted: 1.26M, 1.09M, 1.44M, then 0.96M, the lowest so far. Batch 11 had four fixes, and the others five.

Why it fell from batch 13:

  • No judge ran, so there was no refusal cycle, the judge, repair round and second skeptic that follow a contested fix. That cycle took 455K in batch 13, 6.3% of it, and 2.7% and 5.4% in batches 11 and 12.
  • The skeptics wrote 0.88M less. Batch 13 lost 0.61M to two skeptic runs that a VM restart stopped, and this batch's skeptics averaged 341K a run, against 397K.
  • The workers wrote 0.65M less. No fix measured a half that it then held, as one of batch 13's did for 804K, and the largest fix wrote 545K, against 656K.
  • The cold read was dropped, 168K, and the four closing roles wrote 0.25M less.

Did the process changes pay off? Partly, by the figures. Two changes came before this batch: your narrowing of when a skeptic's edit goes to a judge, and dropping the cold read. Dropping the cold read saved 168K. Under the narrowed rule, three edits that reached outside their fix's files stood without a ruling, and in batch 13 edits like those brought three rulings that cost 455K. Together that's up to about 0.6M a batch, about an eighth of this one.

Against batch 12, the closest match, with five fixes and no restart, this batch wrote 0.61M less, and batch 12's rulings and cold read were 455K of that.

What one batch can't show: most of the 2.4M drop from batch 13 came from things the process didn't change, the restart, the held half and a smaller largest fix. Each fix here also built a decision you'd already answered, with a patch measured in advance, so there was less to dispute. Errors cleared per million tokens fell a little, 6.4 against 6.6 and 9.9 in batches 13 and 12, but that measures what the plan gave the batch. And the new record entries were cut to the record's form after the landing, in a pass whose cost isn't in the 4.82M, so part of the cold read's saving may have moved there. Whether rulings stay at zero, and whether dropping the cold read costs the record anything, needs more batches.

Sources

1. batch-14-review.md, section 2, “Against the record”.

2. The same section, its table by role (batch-measures.py on the four runs). The roles: climb-batch-workflow.md.

3. The same table, “Per rung, all roles” and “Agents, rungs”.

4. The same section, “Why it cost 2.40M less than batch 13”, and Part 2, “The practice's measures, batches 11 to 14”. A refusal cycle's agents: tools/batch-measures.py, line 18.

5. The narrowed rule: commit a1902d0d4, 9 October; the review, Part 2, “The narrowed rule worked”. The cold read gone: CLIMB-BATCH-14.md, section 1, “Cost”. The 0.6M is 168K plus 455K, my sum; the review says batch 13's three rulings were each brought “at least in part” by the old clause, so it's an upper bound.

6. The review, section 2, “Against batch 12”: judges 300K and cold read 155K.

7. The review, section 2, “Sites per million tokens”. The record pass: commit 15a6d4365; its cost isn't measured in any source I read.

How the work was done

Test first held. Every worker's new tests failed through the test runner on the old code before its first edit of source, as its skeptic confirmed from the transcript. Two tests came after an edit, for effects the edit showed, and each failed on the old code. So there was no miss, as in batches 11 to 13.

The skeptics made 19 edits. Two repaired wrong code: the self-type fix looked up a trait from another api in the importing component's names, and the argument retry left out a call that writes its own static arguments, the types in [\ \] brackets. Each of those two started from a test that failed on the worker's code. The other 17 corrected text, tests or records.

No edit was contested, so no judge ran. Three edits reached files outside their fix's list. Each cited the plan's sentence that settles it, as your narrowed rule allows, and stood.

The briefing is the set of decisions, gap rows and specification sections that a fix's plan cites, which the agent prints with the record's search tool before it starts. All ten workers and skeptics ran it as their brief's second step, at their 9th to 11th tool call, and each read every part. None ran it in its first turn, which the brief's order rules out.

Two tool defects showed. First, the batch script told workers that the count stage, the run that measures the count, takes 20 seconds, and ran it in the foreground. Since batch 13b it takes about 5 minutes. One worker's run passed the shell tool's 5-minute limit, and another cut its run and started it again. Climb batch 14's final report: whether it landed, what it changed in Fortress, what it cost, how the work went, what's for your review, and what comes next.

STAMP

The answer

Yes. All five fixes landed on main at 05:34 UTC today (07:34 yours). A fix is one change, built by a worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a skeptic, a second agent that corrects what it finds.

The gate, the full test run before a landing, was green: 1.9K fast tests, 604 system tests and 130 specification examples, with no failure. microGPT's two quick checks under walk, the interpreter, passed 7 of 7 each.

The distance went from 85 to 54, exactly as the batch's plan said. The distance is the number of errors that the checker, the compiled path's type checker, reports on the one library: the interpreter's library, which the compiled path takes over at the switch-over. The count, the older measure that stops at a component's first error, stayed at 1.

It cost 4.82M tokens written, which are input plus cache writes, with cached reads left out. The plan said about 5.9M, and batch 13 cost 7.22M. It ran 4 h 43 min, with 14 agents.

Sources

1. The landing commit 7c2c7cd4b, 05:34 UTC, and its message. The five fixes' own commits: the gather's RECORD.md, “The landed commits”.

2. gate/summary.txt: testFast 1,945 tests in 48 suites, testSystem 604, testSpecData 130, 42 of 42 atomic runs, and the two “microgpt-walk VERDICT: 7 PASS, 0 FAIL of 7” lines.

4. The review, section 2: 4.82M by the coordinator's spend.py, 14 agents, a span of 4 h 43. The plan's figure: CLIMB-BATCH-14.md, section 1, “Cost”.

What changed in Fortress

The checker reads self in a self-typed trait. A self-typed trait is a generic trait whose parameter stands for the type that implements it, like trait StandardTotalOrder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]. In its method bodies the checker now types self as both the trait and T, so the library's opr MAX(self, other: T): T = if other < self then self else other end is accepted, and 29 errors like it went with the library's text unchanged. In return, a type that extends such a trait must be that type: object generator extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\] is refused, since a generator isn't a trip.

The checker retries a call written as another call's argument. When no declaration of a call fits, an argument that's itself a generic call is checked again, with each declaration's parameter type as the type it should produce. So with mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\] and takesBox64(b: BoxT[\ZZ64\]), takesBox64(mk()) now compiles and makes a BoxT[\ZZ64\], where before it was refused. A declaration that fits the arguments as first typed is still never passed over, and no library error moved.

Three library repairs, and one line held. Array2's offset now checks its bounds the way Array1's does, and each fixed-size integer type declares its own numerator: 2 errors went. IntMap's SYMDIFF, the entries in exactly one of two maps, now works with a one-entry map: {0 |-> 0, 1 |-> 1, 2 |-> 2} SYMDIFF {5 |-> 5} holds all four entries, where it held only {2 |-> 2, 5 |-> 5}. The library's big-operator function keeps its one untyped parameter, because walk refuses the typed line.

The 2019 paper's examples are tests, and walk computes powers in sizes. The worked examples of the type group's POPL 2019 paper are now 27 test programs on both paths, the failing ones written as expected failures: tests named XXX that pass while the gap is there. Walk now computes a power in a size, so Box[\2^3\] has size 8, and it refuses a negative exponent, where before it stopped on any power. The specification's No Duplicates Rule now says, as the papers do, that two declarations may not each apply to every call the other applies to; the checker already refused such a pair, like dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\]) beside dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\]).

Walk's rule for an inherited abstract method is coverage. Walk refuses an object at load if it leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, and now the object's bodies at narrower types must together cover the method's parameter types, reading comprises lists, which name every case of a trait. So with trait D comprises { P, Q } and an abstract f(self, other: D), bodies at other: P and other: Q are enough. Before, any one narrower body was, and a call outside it stopped the program at run time; three library places in Random and QuickCheck that leaned on that got their bodies first.

The batch wrote 4.82M tokens. That's 1.08M, or 18%, under the plan's 5.9M, and 2.4M under batch 13.

  • No judge ran, so there was no refusal cycle, the judge, repair round and second skeptic that follow a contested fix. That cycle took 455K in batch 13, 6.3% of it, and 2.7% and 5.4% in batches 11 and 12.

===== s-answer
Yes. All five fixes landed on main at 05:34 UTC today (07:34 yours). A fix is one change, built by a worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a skeptic, a second agent that corrects what it finds.
      The gate, the full test run before a landing, was green: 1.9K fast tests, 604 system tests and 130 specification examples, with no failure. microGPT's two quick checks under walk, the interpreter, passed 7 of 7 each.
      The distance went from 85 to 54, exactly as the batch's plan said. The distance is the number of errors that the checker, the compiled path's type checker, reports on the one library: the interpreter's library, which the compiled path takes over at the switch-over. The count, the older measure that stops at a component's first error, stayed at 1.
      It cost 4.82M tokens written, which are input plus cache writes, with cached reads left out. The plan said about 5.9M, and batch 13 cost 7.22M. It ran 4 h 43 min, with 14 agents.
===== s-fortress
The checker reads self in a self-typed trait. A self-typed trait is a generic trait whose parameter stands for the type that implements it, like trait StandardTotalOrder[\T extends StandardTotalOrder[\T\]\]. In its method bodies the checker now types self as both the trait and T, so the library's opr MAX(self, other: T): T = if other < self then self else other end is accepted, and 29 errors like it went with the library's text unchanged. In return, a type that extends such a trait must be that type: object generator extends StandardTotalOrder[\trip\] is refused, since a generator isn't a trip.
      The checker retries a call written as another call's argument. When no declaration of a call fits, an argument that's itself a generic call is checked again, with each declaration's parameter type as the type it should produce. So with mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\] and takesBox64(b: BoxT[\ZZ64\]), takesBox64(mk()) now compiles and makes a BoxT[\ZZ64\], where before it was refused. A declaration that fits the arguments as first typed is still never passed over, and no library error moved.
      Three library repairs, and one line held. Array2's offset now checks its bounds the way Array1's does, and each fixed-size integer type declares its own numerator: 2 errors went. IntMap's SYMDIFF, the entries in exactly one of two maps, now works with a one-entry map: {0 |-> 0, 1 |-> 1, 2 |-> 2} SYMDIFF {5 |-> 5} holds all four entries, where it held only {2 |-> 2, 5 |-> 5}. The library's big-operator function keeps its one untyped parameter, because walk refuses the typed line.
      The 2019 paper's examples are tests, and walk computes powers in sizes. The worked examples of the type group's POPL 2019 paper are now 27 test programs on both paths, the failing ones written as expected failures: tests named XXX that pass while the gap is there. Walk now computes a power in a size, so Box[\2^3\] has size 8, and it refuses a negative exponent, where before it stopped on any power. The specification's No Duplicates Rule now says, as the papers do, that two declarations may not each apply to every call the other applies to; the checker already refused such a pair, like dup[\T\](x: Box[\T\]) beside dup[\U\](x: Box[\U\]).
      Walk's rule for an inherited abstract method is coverage. Walk refuses an object at load if it leaves an inherited abstract method without a body, and now the object's bodies at narrower types must together cover the method's parameter types, reading comprises lists, which name every case of a trait. So with trait D comprises { P, Q } and an abstract f(self, other: D), bodies at other: P and other: Q are enough. Before, any one narrower body was, and a call outside it stopped the program at run time; three library places in Random and QuickCheck that leaned on that got their bodies first.
===== s-cost
The batch wrote 4.82M tokens. That's 1.08M, or 18%, under the plan's 5.9M, and 2.4M under batch 13.
        By role, for batches 11, 12 and 13, then this one:
          Workers, who build the fixes: 1.99M, 2.05M, 2.64M, then 1.99M.
          Skeptics: 1.60M, 1.67M, 2.59M, then 1.71M.
          Judges, who rule when a skeptic's edit is contested: 140K, 300K, 455K, then none.
          The gather, which lands the approved fixes on main and writes the batch's record: 486K, 527K, 592K, then 460K.

          In all: 5.03M, 5.43M, 7.22M, then 4.82M.

        Why it fell from batch 13:
          No judge ran, so there was no refusal cycle, the judge, repair round and second skeptic that follow a contested fix. That cycle took 455K in batch 13, 6.3% of it, and 2.7% and 5.4% in batches 11 and 12.

      Did the process changes pay off? Partly, by the figures. Two changes came before this batch: your narrowing of when a skeptic's edit goes to a judge, and dropping the cold read. Dropping the cold read saved 168K. Under the narrowed rule, three edits that reached outside their fix's files stood without a ruling, and in batch 13 edits like those brought three rulings that cost 455K.
